recent_posts.content_text:
In our own words
At ILE Labs we build tools. One of them, still under construction and private, led us to this gap: several parties putting together and signing one transaction. When we looked at how CKB’s own multisig payouts and contract upgrades get signed today, we saw the same manual step: signatures pasted into PR comments or chat, checked by eye, then trimmed by hand to exactly the threshold before ckb-cli will send. Fiber’s v0.7.0 upgrade has had enough signatures since 2 November and still isn’t on chain. We had to find out whether the wallets’ formats could be reconciled, so we built a prototype: ckb-msig 0.0.1 checks all six real signatures on that upgrade offline, with no keys and no node. This grant is phase one of the tool: conversion between ckb-cli, Neuron and CCC, and a GitHub Action for signing rounds on pull requests, so that a payout or an upgrade no longer depends on one person editing JSON.
1. Project Overview
What it’s for. When a CKB multisig pays out a grant or upgrades a contract, every signer signs in their own tool. Then one person gathers the signatures by hand from PR comments, chat or files. ckb-msig takes those signatures in whatever form they arrive, tells you which ones are valid for this exact transaction, and writes one file that the next tool, or the chain, accepts.
Who it’s for. The people who sign CKB’s shared money and contract upgrades:
the Spark committee and the Community Fund DAO’s payout signers (2-of-3 wallets);
Fiber’s contract deployers (3-of-5);
teams that keep a treasury in a multisig.
At a glance:
Name: ckb-msig
One line: a command-line tool and GitHub Action that checks, merges and converts partly signed CKB multisig transactions between ckb-cli, Neuron and CCC.
Type: developer tool, open source (MIT), TypeScript, published on npm as @ile_labs/ckb-msig.
Duration: 4 weeks, starting when the grant is approved (the first payment).
Phase: this is phase 1 of ckb-msig. Section 11 sets out what it includes and what comes later.
2. Team Profile
ILE Labs builds open-source tools on CKB. GitHub: ILE-Labs. Nervos Talk: ILE_LABS.
CKB work: fiber-payjoin-kit, an open-source Rust library for collaborative channel funding on Fiber.
Both parties contribute inputs to the funding transaction in a propose, contribute, validate, sign and finalize round trip, tested on a CKB devnet.
It went through a CKBuilders review (CKBuilder-projects#27), where jjyr wrote: “Working at the Cell model / unsigned CellInput is the right approach.”
Why this fits us: fiber-payjoin-kit is the same kind of problem as ckb-msig. Several parties build, check and sign one CKB transaction.
Languages: Rust (fiber-payjoin-kit) and TypeScript (this project, built on CCC).
Availability: 4 weeks from approval, with an update at every weekly check-in.
Contact: email contact@ilelabs.org · Discord emmzy_code01
3. Background
3.1 What it’s for
A signer opens one file and runs one command. They see:
which multisig this is, and which of the three multisig lock deployments it uses;
which signatures are already there;
whether each one is valid for this transaction;
who still has to sign.
The person collecting doesn’t edit JSON. Once enough signatures are in, the tool writes the final transaction. In a repository, the same check runs on every PR comment.
3.2 The problem
Every tool keeps a half-signed transaction differently.
ckb-cli tx files keep the signatures beside the transaction, keyed by lock arg.
ckb-cli deploy files, used for contract upgrades, do the same in another structure. Worse, sign-txs prints a single value where the file expects a list.
Neuron puts the signature bytes in the witness and records who signed in a separate map.
CCC keeps them only in the witness.
What’s already covered: Neuron added a one-way import of ckb-cli tx files in 2024 (neuron#3169).
What isn’t: of the tools we checked, only ckb-cli reads its own deploy files and none converts Neuron files for ckb-cli. Only CCC’s library checks signatures, in code, before someone broadcasts.
ckb-cli wants exactly the threshold. ckb-cli deploy apply-txs refuses anything but exactly M signatures. When five signers answer a 3-of-5 request, someone has to cut the file down to three by hand.
There are three multisig lock deployments in use, and two of the tools know only two of them.
The three are the genesis script, a 2024 deployment that fixes a rare failure, and the 2025 v2 (data1).
ckb-cli and Neuron only know the genesis script and v2.
About 120M CKB in 95 live cells sits under the 2024 deployment (ckb-explorer#2934, janx), and it’s the one UTXO Global’s multisig wallet uses. Signers of those cells can’t use ckb-cli or Neuron.
In the file-based workflows, nobody checks a signature until the chain rejects the transaction. loading, t/8609: “I have checked and all signatures are correct. I don’t understand where my problem is.”
3.3 Evidence of demand
We collected 43 sources from 32 people and teams. The full list, with every quote, the measured timings and how each tool stores signatures, is on the repo’s evidence branch. These are the main ones.
Payouts take days or weeks.
The DAO’s payout to Pocket Node iOS (2-of-3) was started on Aug 21 and completed on Sept 4. zz_tovarishch explained, t/10583/20: “一位委员会成员在 8月21 该项目通过投票后，以2500/$0.00087= 2,873,564 CKB 发起了打款，随后在 9.4 其他委员会成员才完成了多签” (translated: a committee member started the payment on Aug 21 after the vote, and only on Sept 4 did the other members complete the multisig).
It reached the chain on 2026-09-04 at 08:50 UTC, 14 days after it started.
A community member then asked why the CKB amount didn’t match that day’s price (t/10583/19).
The DAO said the same in 2024. JackyLHH, t/7849/1: “This is because DAO’s funds are stored in a multisig wallet, so it takes some time to collect signatures due to timezone and other factors.”
Spark pays every grant from a multisig. The rules say: “Each approved project establishes a multi-signature wallet for Spark funds management and distribution” (t/8752). In July, one grant’s last installment was paid from a personal wallet “因为多签钱包有点问题” (translated: because the multisig wallet had a problem; t/9995/48).
Contract upgrades run through PR comments.
Fiber’s v0.7.0 mainnet upgrade (fiber-scripts #34, 3-of-5): quake asked each signer to run ckb-cli deploy sign-txs and “reply the output in comment:”.
The PR opened on 2026-11-02 at 07:22 UTC.
The third signature came at 09:13 and the fifth on 2026-11-03 at 14:08.
On 2026-11-08 the upgrade still isn’t on chain: both input cells are unspent. We don’t know why, and it may be deliberate.
What the PR does show is four pasted signatures, plus quake’s own already in the file, that one person has to check and merge into mainnet.json, keeping exactly three.
Fiber’s v0.6.0 upgrade reached the chain on 2026-01-14, 22 days after it was prepared (#27, #28). Its signatures were gathered off GitHub.
nostr-binding’s move to new multisig signers took about three weeks over the same holidays (#50, #51).
Core developers asked for it.
doitian, ckb-cli#603 (2024): “Help users to prepare files for requesting multisig signatures from signers. Generate the tx json file and a markdown guidance for signers.” ckb-cli still has no such subcommand.
doitian, ckb-cli#569: “It’s frustrated that sign-txs does not tell how to use the generated signatures”
RetricSu, ckb-cli#658 (2026): “where I sign multisig with ckb-cli without adding the option --add-signature but the info.json still got updated, which is very confused to me.”
Teams keep building their own.
.bit wrote a private signing site for ckb-cli files (dotbitHQ/ckb-multisig-wizard, 2024–25). Its upload check says: “Invalid transaction data, only ckb-cli format is supported.”
kuai (PainterPuppets, kuai#276): “Currently kuai deployment contract only supports local signature deployment, which is a very bad experience when using multiple devices for multi-signature.”
ChainPay (toastmanAu/chain-pay, 2026): “ChainPay coordinates partial signatures.” On the way it “surfaced the witness-padding digest-divergence trap, now fixed”.
UTXO Global runs a hosted multisig wallet with its own backend.
doitian built a browser proof of concept of this idea in 2024 (section 4.3).
Neuron users get stuck.
jordanmack, neuron#2907: “I tried to send and I can’t figure out how to sign and broadcast.”
rink1969, neuron#3260: offline multisig on a transaction that mixed locks ended with “报签名失败” (translated: signing failed).
The DevRel lead is thinking about it. Hanssen, t/10794/5: “I have recently been thinking about using a P2P network to enable a multisignature wallet to manage on-chain assets.”
Other ecosystems:
Bitcoin solved this with one shared format, PSBT (BIP-174), and coordinators such as Caravan.
Ethereum’s Safe has a service for “offchain collecting of signatures”.
CKB has neither. We’re not proposing a new format: ckb-msig converts between the formats CKB wallets already write.
4. Solution
4.1 What it does
Command
What it does
ckb-msig inspect <file> [inputs…]
Detects the format. Shows the multisig (members, threshold, “first n must sign”, which lock deployment). Also checks signatures from other files or pasted sign-txs output, without changing anything. Gives every signature a verdict: valid, duplicate, or not valid for this transaction. When the file names the signer, the last one is split into “signed a different transaction” and “not a member”. Ends with, for example, “2 of 3 valid, waiting for ckb1…”
ckb-msig add <file> <inputs…>
Merges signatures from other files or from pasted sign-txs output, checking each one
ckb-msig convert <file> --to <format>
Writes the same transaction and its valid signatures in another tool’s format: ckb-cli, ckb-cli-deploy, neuron or ccc
ckb-msig finalize <file> [--send <rpc>]
Picks exactly the threshold of valid signatures (respecting “first n”), builds the witness and writes a transaction ready to send. --send broadcasts it
ckb-msig guide <file>
Writes a Markdown note for signers: what the transaction moves (inputs, outputs, capacity, and for upgrades which cells change, with old and new data hashes to compare against the release checksums), and the command to sign it in ckb-cli, Neuron or CCC. This is the “markdown guidance for signers” from ckb-cli#603
GitHub Action
On a PR that carries a ckb-cli deploy file, reads the sign-txs output pasted in comments, checks it, keeps one status comment up to date, and attaches the merged file once the threshold is met
It never holds keys and never signs. Signing stays in ckb-cli, Neuron (including Ledger) and CCC.
4.2 How it’s used
A payout.
The first signer builds the payout in Neuron and exports it.
The second signer works in ckb-cli, runs ckb-msig convert --to ckb-cli, signs, and sends the file back.
ckb-msig add and ckb-msig finalize --send finish the job.
Anyone can run inspect on the final file before it’s sent.
A contract upgrade.
The maintainer opens a PR with the deploy file and the guide output.
Signers paste their sign-txs output, as they did on fiber-scripts #34.
The Action’s comment shows “3 of 5 valid” as soon as it’s true.
The maintainer downloads the merged file and runs ckb-cli deploy apply-txs, or ckb-msig finalize --send.
4.3 What exists, and how this differs
CCC’s multisig signers (Hanssen0, ccc#349, in @ckb-ccc/core since 1.15.0) can sign and aggregate signed copies in code.
ckb-msig is built on them.
What it adds is the file formats, a command line and a CI mode.
If any part belongs in CCC, we’ll offer it there as a PR.
ckb-cli and Neuron keep doing the signing. ckb-msig reads and writes their files. It doesn’t replace their interfaces, hardware wallet support or node access.
Neuron’s ckb-cli import (PR #3169) goes one way and covers tx files only. ckb-msig adds deploy files, the other direction and the 2024 deployment, and it checks signatures first.
doitian’s proof of concept (cryptape/ckb-multisig-cobuild-poc, February–March 2024):
What it does: a browser app that uses CoBuild’s building packet as the exchange format. It reads and writes ckb-cli tx and Neuron files for the genesis script.
Its last commit is 2024-03-05. That’s before the 2024 and v2 deployments and before CCC’s signers.
It shows the conversion works. We’re taking the idea in a different shape: no new exchange format, deploy files included, all three deployments, a command line and a CI mode, and tests on real files.
UTXO Global’s multisig wallet is a hosted site with its own backend.
Signers connect a wallet in the browser.
It’s built on the 2024 deployment and doesn’t read ckb-cli or Neuron files.
ckb-msig runs locally and needs no account or server. It can also check and merge signatures for UTXO Global’s lock.
.bit’s wizard is a self-hosted site with its own database and Ledger signing, for ckb-cli tx files only. Its last commit was in January 2025.
ChainPay is a payroll desktop app that coordinates partial signatures inside its own flow.
What they have in common: each solves the problem for one team or one app. ckb-msig is meant to be the piece they could share: no server, and the files the wallets already write.
Hanssen’s P2P idea: ckb-msig takes a file in and gives a file out, so it doesn’t matter how the file travels. A relay or P2P layer can carry the same data later (section 11).
5. Technical Approach
Stack:
TypeScript on Node 22+, an npm package, and a JavaScript GitHub Action running on Node 24.
Built on @ckb-ccc/core for transaction hashing, the multisig witness codec, the three known multisig scripts and their cell deps, and secp256k1 key recovery.
Structure: four format adapters feed one internal model: the transaction, its input cells when the file carries them, the multisig configs, and the signatures by signer. A verifier and four writers work on that model. The CLI and the Action are thin layers on top.
Facts the design rests on, each checked in the source of ckb-system-scripts, ckb-cli, Neuron and CCC:
The witness lock is the multisig script (S, R, M, N and N key hashes) followed by exactly M 65-byte signatures. Signatures can come in any order, each key counts once, and the first R keys must sign.
The three deployments share that layout, and CCC decodes all three with one codec. They differ in code hash, hash type and cell deps: genesis 0x5c5069eb…e2a8 (type); 2024 0xd1a9f877…c821 (type, testnet 0x765b3ed6…5f09); v2 0x36c971b8…0d29 (data1).
ckb-cli’s build_tx refuses anything but exactly M signatures per multisig lock.
Neuron records the signers’ key hashes in transaction.signatures and the signature bytes in the witness.
The hard part is computing exactly the signing message each tool computes. It covers the transaction hash and the lock group’s witnesses with a placeholder lock, and one byte of difference voids every signature. ChainPay’s notes describe hitting exactly this. That’s why the test files come from each real tool, not from our own encoder.
Offline or not:
Deploy files and Neuron exports carry their input transactions, so they’re checked offline.
ckb-cli tx files and bare CCC transactions need one RPC call to look up input locks.
Limits we’ll document:
A signature doesn’t survive any change to the transaction.
ckb-cli and Neuron can’t sign for the 2024 deployment, so its signers use CCC.
It checks multisig inputs and the ordinary single-key inputs next to them. Other lock types, such as Omnilock, JoyID and anyone-can-pay, are refused in phase 1.
6. To-Do List
Four weeks, five milestones. Each milestone is public and checkable.

7. Required Funding and Breakdown
Total: $2,000, paid in CKB at the rate on the day of approval. All of it is technical work. There are no hosting costs: CI and the Action run on GitHub’s free tier, and testnet CKB comes from the faucet.
Already built before applying, and not charged: the deploy-file reader, the sign-txs parser, signing-message computation and key recovery, the verdicts and lock rules, inspect, and CI. They’re published as the 0.0.1 prototype (section 9).

Why this is more than a standard $1,000 project. The extra cost comes from the number of combinations the tool has to get exactly right, not from extra features:
four formats that store signatures differently: a map keyed by lock arg; a list that must hold exactly M; witness bytes plus a separate signer map; witness only;
three lock deployments with different code hashes, hash types and cell deps, one of which two of the three wallets can’t sign;
two ways to run it: a command line for signers and an Action for repositories;
every path tested on real files made by each tool, and on testnet spends. Neuron is a desktop app, so its files are made by hand.
A $1,000 version would cover ckb-cli and CCC files only, and leave out Neuron, the Action and the signer guide. Those are the parts the payout and upgrade workflows above need.
Payment: 20% at the start. The rest either at the check-ins when M2 and M4 land, or at the end, as the committee prefers.

10. CKB Alignment
It’s built around how multisig works on CKB. A CKB multisig is a lock script, not an account setting. The lock args are a hash of the signer list, the full list travels in the witness, and signing covers a lock group’s witnesses. Getting this right means working with cells, lock groups, witnesses, type and data1 hash types, dep groups and three deployments. None of that carries over from other chains.
It serves CKB’s own governance and infrastructure: Spark and DAO payouts, and contract upgrades through ckb-cli deploy and type id, such as Fiber’s.
It isn’t a Fiber payment tool. It works for any multisig on CKB.
11. Phase 1 and what comes after
This proposal is phase 1 of ckb-msig. It ends at a working command line and GitHub Action for the signing workflows CKB uses today:
In phase 1:
the five commands (inspect, add, convert, finalize, guide);
the four file formats (ckb-cli tx, ckb-cli deploy, Neuron and CCC);
the three multisig deployments;
multisig inputs, with ordinary single-key inputs next to them;
the GitHub Action.
It works on files, never holds keys and never signs.
Left for a later phase:
shared signing sessions over a relay or P2P transport, in line with Hanssen’s idea;
notifications and an audit trail;
a payout mode for grant installments;
other lock types next to multisig: Omnilock (including its multisig mode), JoyID and anyone-can-pay;
time-locked multisig;
an upgrade review view for signers, and hardware wallets through Neuron;
an outside security review.
The next phase will take these up, shaped by what phase 1’s users ask for.
Questions we expect
Why not just use CCC? CCC is a library, and ckb-msig uses it. Signers who work in ckb-cli or Neuron can’t call a library, and CCC doesn’t read their files, run from a terminal or check PR comments.
Neuron already imports ckb-cli files. Isn’t this solved? Partly. It imports ckb-cli tx files only, one way. It doesn’t read deploy files, which is what contract upgrades use, and ckb-cli can’t read Neuron’s files back. Neither tool knows the 2024 deployment, and neither checks signatures before broadcasting.
doitian built this in 2024. Why build it again? That proof of concept showed the conversion works. It stopped there in March 2024, before two of the three deployments and before CCC’s signers existed. We’re building on the same idea as a command line and CI tool, with deploy files and tests on real files.
Is it safe to use on treasury money?
It holds no keys and can’t sign.
convert doesn’t change the transaction. Its output keeps the input’s transaction hash, and the tests check this on every file.
A signature made on any other transaction is flagged, and the chain checks every signature again.
inspect and guide show the transaction hash and what the transaction moves, so signers can compare before they sign. Each signer still reviews it in their own wallet.
The final transaction is a plain file anyone can inspect before it’s sent.
Isn’t multisig still changing? Not in the part this tool depends on. The witness layout is the same across all three deployments. The changes since 2024 fixed verification and since handling, and one more since change is still open (ckb-system-scripts#106). A new deployment would be one more row in a table.
Who uses it first? Any repository that deploys with ckb-cli and a multisig can add the Action. Anyone paying out from a multisig can run inspect on the files they already pass around.

3. Background

3.1 What it’s for

A signer opens one file and runs one command. They see:

  • which multisig this is, and which of the three multisig lock deployments it uses;
  • which signatures are already there;
  • whether each one is valid for this transaction;
  • who still has to sign.

The person collecting doesn’t edit JSON. Once enough signatures are in, the tool writes the final transaction. In a repository, the same check runs on every PR comment.

3.2 The problem

  1. Every tool keeps a half-signed transaction differently.
    • ckb-cli tx files keep the signatures beside the transaction, keyed by lock arg.
    • ckb-cli deploy files, used for contract upgrades, do the same in another structure. Worse, sign-txs prints a single value where the file expects a list.
    • Neuron puts the signature bytes in the witness and records who signed in a separate map.
    • CCC keeps them only in the witness.
    • What’s already covered: Neuron added a one-way import of ckb-cli tx files in 2024 (neuron#3169).
    • What isn’t: of the tools we checked, only ckb-cli reads its own deploy files and none converts Neuron files for ckb-cli. Only CCC’s library checks signatures, in code, before someone broadcasts.
  2. ckb-cli wants exactly the threshold. ckb-cli deploy apply-txs refuses anything but exactly M signatures. When five signers answer a 3-of-5 request, someone has to cut the file down to three by hand.
  3. There are three multisig lock deployments in use, and two of the tools know only two of them.
    • The three are the genesis script, a 2024 deployment that fixes a rare failure, and the 2025 v2 (data1).
    • ckb-cli and Neuron only know the genesis script and v2.
    • About 120M CKB in 95 live cells sits under the 2024 deployment (ckb-explorer#2934, janx), and it’s the one UTXO Global’s multisig wallet uses. Signers of those cells can’t use ckb-cli or Neuron.
  4. In the file-based workflows, nobody checks a signature until the chain rejects the transaction. loading, t/8609: “I have checked and all signatures are correct. I don’t understand where my problem is.”

3.3 Evidence of demand

We collected 43 sources from 32 people and teams. The full list, with every quote, the measured timings and how each tool stores signatures, is on the repo’s evidence branch. These are the main ones.

Payouts take days or weeks.

  • The DAO’s payout to Pocket Node iOS (2-of-3) was started on Aug 21 and completed on Sept 4. zz_tovarishch explained, t/10583/20: “一位委员会成员在 8月21 该项目通过投票后，以2500/$0.00087= 2,873,564 CKB 发起了打款，随后在 9.4 其他委员会成员才完成了多签” (translated: a committee member started the payment on Aug 21 after the vote, and only on Sept 4 did the other members complete the multisig).
    • It reached the chain on 2026-09-04 at 08:50 UTC, 14 days after it started.
    • A community member then asked why the CKB amount didn’t match that day’s price (t/10583/19).
  • The DAO said the same in 2024. JackyLHH, t/7849/1: “This is because DAO’s funds are stored in a multisig wallet, so it takes some time to collect signatures due to timezone and other factors.”
  • Spark pays every grant from a multisig. The rules say: “Each approved project establishes a multi-signature wallet for Spark funds management and distribution” (t/8752). In July, one grant’s last installment was paid from a personal wallet “因为多签钱包有点问题” (translated: because the multisig wallet had a problem; t/9995/48).

Contract upgrades run through PR comments.

  • Fiber’s v0.7.0 mainnet upgrade (fiber-scripts #34, 3-of-5): quake asked each signer to run ckb-cli deploy sign-txs and “reply the output in comment:”.
    • The PR opened on 2026-11-02 at 07:22 UTC.
    • The third signature came at 09:13 and the fifth on 2026-11-03 at 14:08.
    • On 2026-11-08 the upgrade still isn’t on chain: both input cells are unspent. We don’t know why, and it may be deliberate.
    • What the PR does show is four pasted signatures, plus quake’s own already in the file, that one person has to check and merge into mainnet.json, keeping exactly three.
  • Fiber’s v0.6.0 upgrade reached the chain on 2026-01-14, 22 days after it was prepared (#27, #28). Its signatures were gathered off GitHub.
  • nostr-binding’s move to new multisig signers took about three weeks over the same holidays (#50, #51).

Core developers asked for it.

  • doitian, ckb-cli#603 (2024): “Help users to prepare files for requesting multisig signatures from signers. Generate the tx json file and a markdown guidance for signers.” ckb-cli still has no such subcommand.
  • doitian, ckb-cli#569: “It’s frustrated that sign-txs does not tell how to use the generated signatures”
  • RetricSu, ckb-cli#658 (2026): “where I sign multisig with ckb-cli without adding the option --add-signature but the info.json still got updated, which is very confused to me.”

Teams keep building their own.

  • .bit wrote a private signing site for ckb-cli files (dotbitHQ/ckb-multisig-wizard, 2024–25). Its upload check says: “Invalid transaction data, only ckb-cli format is supported.”
  • kuai (PainterPuppets, kuai#276): “Currently kuai deployment contract only supports local signature deployment, which is a very bad experience when using multiple devices for multi-signature.”
  • ChainPay (toastmanAu/chain-pay, 2026): “ChainPay coordinates partial signatures.” On the way it “surfaced the witness-padding digest-divergence trap, now fixed”.
  • UTXO Global runs a hosted multisig wallet with its own backend.
  • doitian built a browser proof of concept of this idea in 2024 (section 4.3).

Neuron users get stuck.

  • jordanmack, neuron#2907: “I tried to send and I can’t figure out how to sign and broadcast.”
  • rink1969, neuron#3260: offline multisig on a transaction that mixed locks ended with “报签名失败” (translated: signing failed).

The DevRel lead is thinking about it. Hanssen, t/10794/5: “I have recently been thinking about using a P2P network to enable a multisignature wallet to manage on-chain assets.”

Other ecosystems:

  • Bitcoin solved this with one shared format, PSBT (BIP-174), and coordinators such as Caravan.
  • Ethereum’s Safe has a service for “offchain collecting of signatures”.
  • CKB has neither. We’re not proposing a new format: ckb-msig converts between the formats CKB wallets already write.

4. Solution

4.1 What it does

Command What it does
ckb-msig inspect <file> [inputs…] Detects the format. Shows the multisig (members, threshold, “first n must sign”, which lock deployment). Also checks signatures from other files or pasted sign-txs output, without changing anything. Gives every signature a verdict: valid, duplicate, or not valid for this transaction. When the file names the signer, the last one is split into “signed a different transaction” and “not a member”. Ends with, for example, “2 of 3 valid, waiting for ckb1…”
ckb-msig add <file> <inputs…> Merges signatures from other files or from pasted sign-txs output, checking each one
ckb-msig convert <file> --to <format> Writes the same transaction and its valid signatures in another tool’s format: ckb-cli, ckb-cli-deploy, neuron or ccc
ckb-msig finalize <file> [--send <rpc>] Picks exactly the threshold of valid signatures (respecting “first n”), builds the witness and writes a transaction ready to send. --send broadcasts it
ckb-msig guide <file> Writes a Markdown note for signers: what the transaction moves (inputs, outputs, capacity, and for upgrades which cells change, with old and new data hashes to compare against the release checksums), and the command to sign it in ckb-cli, Neuron or CCC. This is the “markdown guidance for signers” from ckb-cli#603
GitHub Action On a PR that carries a ckb-cli deploy file, reads the sign-txs output pasted in comments, checks it, keeps one status comment up to date, and attaches the merged file once the threshold is met

It never holds keys and never signs. Signing stays in ckb-cli, Neuron (including Ledger) and CCC.

4.2 How it’s used

A payout.

  1. The first signer builds the payout in Neuron and exports it.
  2. The second signer works in ckb-cli, runs ckb-msig convert --to ckb-cli, signs, and sends the file back.
  3. ckb-msig add and ckb-msig finalize --send finish the job.
  4. Anyone can run inspect on the final file before it’s sent.

A contract upgrade.

  1. The maintainer opens a PR with the deploy file and the guide output.
  2. Signers paste their sign-txs output, as they did on fiber-scripts #34.
  3. The Action’s comment shows “3 of 5 valid” as soon as it’s true.
  4. The maintainer downloads the merged file and runs ckb-cli deploy apply-txs, or ckb-msig finalize --send.

4.3 What exists, and how this differs

  • CCC’s multisig signers (Hanssen0, ccc#349, in @ckb-ccc/core since 1.15.0) can sign and aggregate signed copies in code.
    • ckb-msig is built on them.
    • What it adds is the file formats, a command line and a CI mode.
    • If any part belongs in CCC, we’ll offer it there as a PR.
  • ckb-cli and Neuron keep doing the signing. ckb-msig reads and writes their files. It doesn’t replace their interfaces, hardware wallet support or node access.
  • Neuron’s ckb-cli import (PR #3169) goes one way and covers tx files only. ckb-msig adds deploy files, the other direction and the 2024 deployment, and it checks signatures first.
  • doitian’s proof of concept (cryptape/ckb-multisig-cobuild-poc, February–March 2024):
    • What it does: a browser app that uses CoBuild’s building packet as the exchange format. It reads and writes ckb-cli tx and Neuron files for the genesis script.
    • Its last commit is 2024-03-05. That’s before the 2024 and v2 deployments and before CCC’s signers.
    • It shows the conversion works. We’re taking the idea in a different shape: no new exchange format, deploy files included, all three deployments, a command line and a CI mode, and tests on real files.
  • UTXO Global’s multisig wallet is a hosted site with its own backend.
    • Signers connect a wallet in the browser.
    • It’s built on the 2024 deployment and doesn’t read ckb-cli or Neuron files.
    • ckb-msig runs locally and needs no account or server. It can also check and merge signatures for UTXO Global’s lock.
  • .bit’s wizard is a self-hosted site with its own database and Ledger signing, for ckb-cli tx files only. Its last commit was in January 2025.
  • ChainPay is a payroll desktop app that coordinates partial signatures inside its own flow.
  • What they have in common: each solves the problem for one team or one app. ckb-msig is meant to be the piece they could share: no server, and the files the wallets already write.
  • Hanssen’s P2P idea: ckb-msig takes a file in and gives a file out, so it doesn’t matter how the file travels. A relay or P2P layer can carry the same data later (section 11).

5. Technical Approach

  • Stack:
    • TypeScript on Node 22+, an npm package, and a JavaScript GitHub Action running on Node 24.
    • Built on @ckb-ccc/core for transaction hashing, the multisig witness codec, the three known multisig scripts and their cell deps, and secp256k1 key recovery.
  • Structure: four format adapters feed one internal model: the transaction, its input cells when the file carries them, the multisig configs, and the signatures by signer. A verifier and four writers work on that model. The CLI and the Action are thin layers on top.
  • Facts the design rests on, each checked in the source of ckb-system-scripts, ckb-cli, Neuron and CCC:
    • The witness lock is the multisig script (S, R, M, N and N key hashes) followed by exactly M 65-byte signatures. Signatures can come in any order, each key counts once, and the first R keys must sign.
    • The three deployments share that layout, and CCC decodes all three with one codec. They differ in code hash, hash type and cell deps: genesis 0x5c5069eb…e2a8 (type); 2024 0xd1a9f877…c821 (type, testnet 0x765b3ed6…5f09); v2 0x36c971b8…0d29 (data1).
    • ckb-cli’s build_tx refuses anything but exactly M signatures per multisig lock.
    • Neuron records the signers’ key hashes in transaction.signatures and the signature bytes in the witness.
  • The hard part is computing exactly the signing message each tool computes. It covers the transaction hash and the lock group’s witnesses with a placeholder lock, and one byte of difference voids every signature. ChainPay’s notes describe hitting exactly this. That’s why the test files come from each real tool, not from our own encoder.
  • Offline or not:
    • Deploy files and Neuron exports carry their input transactions, so they’re checked offline.
    • ckb-cli tx files and bare CCC transactions need one RPC call to look up input locks.
  • Limits we’ll document:
    • A signature doesn’t survive any change to the transaction.
    • ckb-cli and Neuron can’t sign for the 2024 deployment, so its signers use CCC.
    • It checks multisig inputs and the ordinary single-key inputs next to them. Other lock types, such as Omnilock, JoyID and anyone-can-pay, are refused in phase 1.

6. To-Do List

Four weeks, five milestones. Each milestone is public and checkable.

Week Work Milestone
1 Three 2-of-3 multisigs on testnet (genesis, 2024, v2), funded from the faucet. Partly signed files made with ckb-cli (tx and deploy), Neuron and CCC. A page on how each tool stores signatures. Test what Neuron does with a ckb-cli file for a v2 multisig M1: test files and format page public
2 Readers for ckb-cli tx files, Neuron and CCC (the deploy-file reader already exists), input lookup over RPC, and the specific verdicts when a file names the signer. add and convert with four writers, exact-threshold selection with “first n”, and round-trip tests M2: v0.1.0-alpha on npm
3 finalize and --send. Three testnet spends, one per deployment, with signatures from different tools wherever they support that deployment (only CCC signs for the 2024 one). Start the GitHub Action M3: three testnet tx hashes in the README
4 Finish the GitHub Action, and a demo repo that replays the fiber-scripts #34 workflow on testnet. guide, docs, fixes from the weekly check-ins, video, v0.1.0, final report M4: demo PR with the Action’s comment. M5: release and report

7. Required Funding and Breakdown

Total: $2,000, paid in CKB at the rate on the day of approval. All of it is technical work. There are no hosting costs: CI and the Action run on GitHub’s free tier, and testnet CKB comes from the faucet.

Already built before applying, and not charged: the deploy-file reader, the sign-txs parser, signing-message computation and key recovery, the verdicts and lock rules, inspect, and CI. They’re published as the 0.0.1 prototype (section 9).

Remaining work USD
Test files from real tools on testnet, and the format page 360
Readers for ckb-cli tx, Neuron and CCC files; input lookup over RPC; signer-specific verdicts 280
add, convert, finalize, --send 360
Tests for the new readers, writers and commands 150
Three testnet spends across tools 150
GitHub Action and demo repo 330
guide 150
Docs, video, release, weekly updates and final report 220
Total 2,000

Each line pays for one deliverable in section 8, and nothing already built is charged again.

Why this is more than a standard $1,000 project. The extra cost comes from the number of combinations the tool has to get exactly right, not from extra features:

  • four formats that store signatures differently: a map keyed by lock arg; a list that must hold exactly M; witness bytes plus a separate signer map; witness only;
  • three lock deployments with different code hashes, hash types and cell deps, one of which two of the three wallets can’t sign;
  • two ways to run it: a command line for signers and an Action for repositories;
  • every path tested on real files made by each tool, and on testnet spends. Neuron is a desktop app, so its files are made by hand.

A $1,000 version would cover ckb-cli and CCC files only, and leave out Neuron, the Action and the signer guide. Those are the parts the payout and upgrade workflows above need.

Payment: 20% at the start. The rest either at the check-ins when M2 and M4 land, or at the end, as the committee prefers.

8. Deliverables and How to Verify

A. Deliverables

# Deliverable Done when
1 Public repo ILE-Labs/ckb-msig (MIT) and npm package @ile_labs/ckb-msig v0.1.0 The tag exists, CI is green on it, and npx @ile_labs/ckb-msig --help lists the five commands
2 Readers and writers for ckb-cli tx, ckb-cli deploy, Neuron and CCC files Round-trip tests pass on every test file: read, write and read again gives the same transaction and signatures
3 Verification for the three deployments inspect gives the right verdict on test files with valid, wrong-transaction, non-member and duplicate signatures
4 Test files from real tools fixtures/ holds partly signed files made on testnet by ckb-cli, Neuron and CCC (ckb-cli and Neuron only for the deployments they support), plus the public fiber-scripts #34 file, downloaded from a pinned commit and checked by SHA-256, and its posted signatures
5 Testnet spends across tools The README lists three testnet tx hashes, one per deployment, each spending a 2-of-3 multisig cell, with the tool behind each signature
6 GitHub Action and demo repo A public demo PR replays the fiber-scripts #34 workflow on testnet: signers paste sign-txs output, the Action’s comment gives each signature’s verdict, and the final transaction is on testnet
7 guide The guide for the demo PR is committed and shows the cells that change and their data hashes
8 Docs and video A README covering every command, a page on how each tool stores signatures and what can’t be converted, and a video of five minutes or less

B. How to verify, without reading the code

  1. CI: open the repo’s Actions tab. The run on tag v0.1.0 is green. Locally, npm ci && npm test gives the same result.
  2. Real mainnet data, no keys and no node: run npm run fixtures:fetch && npx @ile_labs/ckb-msig@0.1.0 inspect fixtures/fiber-scripts-34/mainnet.json fixtures/fiber-scripts-34/comments/*. The first command downloads the fiber-scripts #34 file from a pinned commit and checks its SHA-256. Expected: the 3-of-5 multisig (v2, data1), its five members, and a verdict for each posted signature.
  3. Testnet spends: open the three tx hashes from the README in the testnet explorer. Each one spends a 2-of-3 multisig cell of the stated deployment.
  4. The Action: open the demo PR. The Action’s comment lists the valid and rejected signatures with the reason, and links the final testnet transaction.
  5. The video.

Environment: Node 22+ on Linux, macOS or Windows, for steps 1 and 2 only. No CKB node is needed. All five checks take under 15 minutes.

9. Current State vs. Funded Work

Today Funded by Spark
Research 47 sources of demand, four timed signing flows, and how each tool stores signatures, checked in the source code. All public on the repo’s evidence branch A format page in the main docs, kept up to date
Repo ILE-Labs/ckb-msig: README, MIT license, CI on Node 22 and 24, and the v0.0.1 release The rest of the tool, released as v0.1.0
Code A working inspect for ckb-cli deploy files, published on npm as @ile_labs/ckb-msig@0.0.1. On the fiber-scripts #34 deploy file it finds all six real signatures valid and reports the upgrade ready (5 valid, 3 needed), offline and with no keys. 154 tests The other four commands, the other three formats, the GitHub Action
Test files The fiber-scripts #34 mainnet file (a pinned download, checked by SHA-256) and its four posted signatures Real testnet files from each tool for the three deployments
Proof Anyone can run npx @ile_labs/ckb-msig@0.0.1 inspect <deploy file> today Three testnet tx hashes, a demo PR, a video

10. CKB Alignment

  • It’s built around how multisig works on CKB. A CKB multisig is a lock script, not an account setting. The lock args are a hash of the signer list, the full list travels in the witness, and signing covers a lock group’s witnesses. Getting this right means working with cells, lock groups, witnesses, type and data1 hash types, dep groups and three deployments. None of that carries over from other chains.
  • It serves CKB’s own governance and infrastructure: Spark and DAO payouts, and contract upgrades through ckb-cli deploy and type id, such as Fiber’s.
  • It isn’t a Fiber payment tool. It works for any multisig on CKB.

11. Phase 1 and what comes after

This proposal is phase 1 of ckb-msig. It ends at a working command line and GitHub Action for the signing workflows CKB uses today:

  • In phase 1:

    • the five commands (inspect, add, convert, finalize, guide);
    • the four file formats (ckb-cli tx, ckb-cli deploy, Neuron and CCC);
    • the three multisig deployments;
    • multisig inputs, with ordinary single-key inputs next to them;
    • the GitHub Action.

    It works on files, never holds keys and never signs.

  • Left for a later phase:

    • shared signing sessions over a relay or P2P transport, in line with Hanssen’s idea;
    • notifications and an audit trail;
    • a payout mode for grant installments;
    • other lock types next to multisig: Omnilock (including its multisig mode), JoyID and anyone-can-pay;
    • time-locked multisig;
    • an upgrade review view for signers, and hardware wallets through Neuron;
    • an outside security review.

The next phase will take these up, shaped by what phase 1’s users ask for.

Questions we expect

Why not just use CCC? CCC is a library, and ckb-msig uses it. Signers who work in ckb-cli or Neuron can’t call a library, and CCC doesn’t read their files, run from a terminal or check PR comments.

Neuron already imports ckb-cli files. Isn’t this solved? Partly. It imports ckb-cli tx files only, one way. It doesn’t read deploy files, which is what contract upgrades use, and ckb-cli can’t read Neuron’s files back. Neither tool knows the 2024 deployment, and neither checks signatures before broadcasting.

doitian built this in 2024. Why build it again? That proof of concept showed the conversion works. It stopped there in March 2024, before two of the three deployments and before CCC’s signers existed. We’re building on the same idea as a command line and CI tool, with deploy files and tests on real files.

Is it safe to use on treasury money?

  • It holds no keys and can’t sign.
  • convert doesn’t change the transaction. Its output keeps the input’s transaction hash, and the tests check this on every file.
  • A signature made on any other transaction is flagged, and the chain checks every signature again.
  • inspect and guide show the transaction hash and what the transaction moves, so signers can compare before they sign. Each signer still reviews it in their own wallet.
  • The final transaction is a plain file anyone can inspect before it’s sent.

Isn’t multisig still changing? Not in the part this tool depends on. The witness layout is the same across all three deployments. The changes since 2024 fixed verification and since handling, and one more since change is still open (ckb-system-scripts#106). A new deployment would be one more row in a table.

Who uses it first? Any repository that deploys with ckb-cli and a multisig can add the Action. Anyone paying out from a multisig can run inspect on the files they already pass around.

recent_posts.content_text:
Thanks for reading it this closely, and for the ideas.
Voting is actually something I’ve spent a lot of time on. Earlier this year I built a ZK voting system for the Buidl Guidl challenge, and I wrote up everything that broke along the way: Anonymous Blockchain Voting is Impossible (I Was Wrong)
The main thing I took from that was that the proof on its own doesn’t give you private voting. You need a commitment tree so people can prove they’re registered without saying which registration is theirs, a nullifier per election so nobody votes twice and you can’t follow the same voter across elections, and something like a paymaster, because the moment the voter’s own account pays the fee, everything you hid with the proof is linked back to them. So the tally today only covers one piece of that. It keeps a value hidden and binds each update to one exact Cell transition, but it doesn’t do the membership or the unlinking yet.
Your version is also a bit different from what I built. In mine, the votes themselves were public, and only the voter was hidden. You want the tally to stay hidden until a disclosure step, which is a harder problem. How are you thinking about that part: threshold decryption, commit-and-reveal, something else?
On the fee payer, yes, that’s how I read it too. The proof covers the consumed Cell, the old and new commitments, and the new Cell’s lock and capacity, but not the fee inputs. So a relayer should be able to add its own CKB to pay without being able to change anything about the tally. Basically the CKB version of the paymaster problem. I want to add a test for exactly that before I claim it publicly, one where a different account pays and one where someone tries to change the tally output. I’ll also look at Service Runner as a place where a relayer like that could live.
The part I think will be hardest on CKB is the shared state. A commitment tree and a nullifier set mean lots of people trying to update the same Cells, and I haven’t seen a good answer for that yet. Would love to hear if you’ve thought about it for voting.
And the node operators idea for ceremonies is a really good one. Contributors with something at stake would be much stronger than whoever happened to see my post. I’ll keep it in mind for the next one.

recent_posts.content_text:
xiaomao:
Voting
Hi xiaomao,
Thanks for the thoughtful reply, and for the write-up on what broke in your Buidl Guidl system. Your three ingredients (commitment tree, per-election nullifier, paymaster) are exactly the list I keep landing on too.
Some context, so you know where I stand. For about a year and a half I have been working on VoteSecure, a private voting app on CKB (site: votesecure.net, code: GitHub - psawyerberlin/votesecure: VoteSecure is a decentralized application (dApp) for running transparent, tamper evident, and privacy preserving elections and polls. The application is open source and designed so results can be independently audited without trusting a central authority. · GitHub). To be upfront: the prototype in the repo follows an old v1 design, and its script still accepts every transaction. The current spec (v2.3) is a work in progress with several open problems still to solve.
Your question: how the tally stays hidden until disclosure. My first answer was drand. Each event had one tally key, timelock-encrypted to a future drand round, so nobody could read the ballots before release. I dropped it for two reasons. Once the round passed, anyone could decrypt every individual ballot. And whoever generated the key could peek before release.
The current idea is threshold decryption plus homomorphic tallying:
Each ballot is one exponential-ElGamal ciphertext per option, under a key generated jointly by t-of-n trustees. Nobody ever holds the whole key. Escrow applications depend on transaction validation rules that must remain correct even when users construct unexpected or malicious transactions.
A script may appear to work under normal conditions but still contain weaknesses involving unauthorized releases, invalid state transitions, recipient redirection, repeated settlement attempts, or incorrect accounting across multiple cells.

Instead, it addresses a narrower developer tooling opportunity: providing a documented, reproducible set of adversarial transaction tests and reference security invariants that escrow developers can adapt when testing their own implementations.

A. Reusable Rust Security Test Suite
A collection of transaction-level test fixtures designed to examine common escrow security properties.

Unauthorized release: Verify that an escrow cannot be released without the required authorization. Double release and replay: Verify that a completed milestone or escrow cannot be settled more than once. State integrity: Verify that milestone states cannot be reset, skipped, or changed through invalid transitions. Recipient integrity: Verify that funds cannot be redirected to an unauthorized recipient. Timeout enforcement: Verify that refunds are permitted only under the defined timeout conditions and that premature refunds are rejected. Transaction isolation and accounting: Verify that multiple escrow cells, unrelated transaction inputs, and outputs cannot be used to bypass escrow-specific accounting rules.
The tests will construct complete CKB transactions and verify their execution using the established CKB testing workflow.
B. Minimal Rust Reference Escrow Script
We will implement a small reference escrow script to demonstrate the security rules being tested.
The reference implementation will support:
Escrow creation with defined participants and conditions. Authorized milestone release. State transition validation. Timeout-based refunds. Native CKB capacity accounting. Validation of relevant transaction inputs and outputs.
The implementation will deliberately remain limited. It will not include a marketplace, dispute-resolution interface, multisignature system, governance module, or production fund-management service.
A deliberately vulnerable reference variant will also be included for selected test cases. This will demonstrate that the attack scenarios are meaningful: the vulnerable implementation should accept the relevant attack, while the protected implementation should reject it.

How the test suite is structured. How to run the tests locally. How to add a new adversarial transaction scenario. How the reference escrow script enforces its security conditions. How developers can adapt the test patterns to their own escrow scripts. How to reproduce the testnet demonstration.

The documentation will distinguish between properties demonstrated by the reference implementation and properties that must be independently verified in an external project.

The initial reference implementation will use a defined set of escrow participants, release conditions, and timeout rules.
Lock arguments: Store or commit to the authorization identity, refund recipient, timeout configuration, and escrow configuration reference.
Cell data: Represent the escrow’s current state and milestone information. Native CKB capacity will represent the locked value.
Release validation: Require the specified authorization and a valid state transition. Validate the relevant transaction structure and destination conditions.

All source code, test cases, and documentation produced through the grant will be publicly accessible.

The Rust reference script builds successfully. The security test suite executes through the documented CKB testing workflow. Each of the six attack categories has a reproducible transaction-level test. Selected attacks succeed against the deliberately vulnerable reference variant and are rejected by the protected implementation. Thanks for going through the code carefully @ArthurZhang. Every point you raised was real. Here is what changed since 514c33a through 79788a8 (both directly from your notes and a few fixes around them):
1. Same hash algorithm on both legs
Removed the hardcoded SHA-256 constant.
Invoice parsing now reads hash_algorithm from /data/attrs, defaults to ckb_hash when omitted (matching Fiber v0.9.1), and rejects unknown or conflicting values.
Before creating a hold, the daemon rejects unsupported algorithms on the buyer’s invoice, passes that invoice’s hash_algorithm to new_invoice for the hold, and verifies the created hold invoice matches it.
Both replacement invoices and on_payout_status check that the payout invoice’s hash_algorithm still matches the hold’s algorithm.
2. Anchoring outgoing tlc_expiry_limit to the actual incoming TLC
Instead of estimating remaining time from hold_received_at + hold_secs, inbound_tlc_expiry now queries list_channels (include_closed: true) for the earliest live, non-forwarded Inbound pending TLC matching the hold’s payment_hash (skipping Outbound, forwarded entries with forwarding_channel_id, and LocalRemoved / RemoveAckConfirmed), and persists that in hold_expires_at_ms.
Both Received and Paid hold transitions wait until an inbound TLC expiry is found before opening the fiat window (and missing expiry on an already-open hold is backfilled, or triggers a refund on payout instead of falling back to Fiber’s 14-day max).
The parser now reads final_htlc_minimum_expiry_delta (defaulting to Fiber’s 24h when omitted, rejecting conflicts). recent_posts.author: mulham_na
recent_posts.content_text:
Hi everyone! I’ve been working on @fiber-pay/react-native for my CKBuilders capstone and wanted to share where it stands.
The idea came from looking at khie-mobile, a React Native wallet for CKB. It doesn’t support Fiber payments yet. fiber-pay already has React hooks, but those run a Fiber node in the browser through WASM and IndexedDB, so they don’t fit React Native. When I read through @fiber-pay/sdk, I found that its FiberRpcClient only needs fetch. That meant I could use the existing client and connect to a remote fnn node over JSON-RPC, instead of trying to run a node on the phone.
The package has two hooks so far:
useFiberNode({ url }) connects to the node and exposes its status and RPC client.
useFiberPayment(client) creates and parses invoices, and can send a payment and wait for its result.
I tested the node connection and invoice creation/parsing against a live testnet fnn node. The full payment flow has unit tests, but I haven’t completed a live payment between two nodes yet. I also added a standalone demo screen in khie-mobile and checked it against the app’s actual stack: typecheck, all 102 existing tests, and a Metro bundle passed. The screen isn’t wired into the app’s navigation yet, and I haven’t run it on a device.
The upstream PR is still a draft: feat(react-native): add React Native client for Fiber Network by mulhamna · Pull Request #205 · RetricSu/fiber-pay · GitHub. I wrote up the work and the snags along the way in my weekly reports.
I’d especially appreciate feedback on using a remote node for a wallet client, and on what would make this useful in khie-mobile beyond the demo screen.

recent_posts.author: psawyerberlin
recent_posts.content_text:
Ticoworld:
QuotaCell delegate key, without needing access to the owner’s key?
Thanks @Ticoworld, and sorry for the slow follow-up. I wanted to check this properly against how CSR actually works before answering.
The honest answer: yes, technically, but it doesn’t add much.
A CSR job can’t carry a key of its own. Every CSR runner signs its transactions with its own service key, and services never see that key. So the only way to use a QuotaCell delegate today would be to register one specific runner’s key as the delegate. The owner’s key would never be needed, but the refill would then depend on that single runner being online.
That’s essentially what Ayoub already has with his keeper bot, just running somewhere else. The value of CSR is that any node can execute a job, and a fixed delegate key removes exactly that. So I have to be honest: with the current delegate design, CSR isn’t really a good fit for the refill.
An idea, if you find it interesting: no delegate key at all
Since the recipient (the keeper) and the amount are fixed, the Pocket could in principle offer a keyless refill rule: “anyone may move exactly Y to the keeper address, at most once every N blocks.”
The funds can only ever go to the keeper.
The cooldown and the Pocket’s cap limit how much can move.
There is no delegate key to protect.
The owner keeps full control.
The “keeper below X” check would then run as a small CSR job that any node can pick up, with no single bot or server to keep alive.
I haven’t checked whether something like this fits into Q’s design, or what trade-offs it brings, so please take it only as a suggestion. You know the policy much better than I do.
Either way, thanks for the open discussion, and I’m happy to help test if a direction emerges where CSR makes sense. I’m also on Telegram: View @ckbrunner if you’d like to talk it through.
